t: AI Weekly: Micron boosts chip stocks, firms mull AI-related cuts
desc: STORY: From chip stocks getting a fresh boost... to where chip workers have become among the most desirable partners.. This is AI Weekly.:: AI WeeklyChip stocks rebounded after bullish outlooks from U.S. firms Micron Technology and Qualcomm.Micron said customers had committed to spend $22 billion on its chips.It also forecast quarterly profit and revenue well above expectations, sending its shares 12% higher in after-hours trading.Landsberg Bennett Chief Investment Officer Michael Landsberg says the AI boom has been transformational for memory chip makers like Micron:“What’s happened in this space has been, typically this used to be more of a commodity, and so what’s happened now with AI, a lot of these chips are needed to make AI work faster and better so the demand has really been strong across the entire sector.”Donald Trump has said Apple has agreed to work with Intel to design and manufacture its chips in the U.S.The move would be a major boost for the American chipmaker's efforts to turn around its business.A contract with Apple would lock in steady demand from the iPhone maker.That would boost Intel's reputation and sales as it looks to close the gap with rival TSMC.Oracle's total workforce declined 13%, or about 21,000 employees, in its fiscal 2026.It's as the cloud computing giant continued restructuring its business... partly driven by the adoption of AI across its operations.Up to 3,000 Santander employees in Spain could also be offered early retirement.That's as the bank braces for impacts brought on by AI, Spanish newspaper Expansion reported on Wednesday.SK Hynix overtook Samsung Electronics to become South Korea's most valuable listed company.Shares in what is now the world's most valuable memory chipmaker rose to bring the company's market capitalization to $1.35 trillion. Employees at chip factories are also now part of South Korea’s A-list. Some workers at Samsung’s chip division are set for bonuses of about $416,000.Around 14 times South Korea’s average annual salary.Chip workers now rival doctors and lawyers as the nation’s most desirable partners.Lee Sung-mi from matchmaking agency Sunoo says tech staffers now rate very highly:"Scores for Samsung Electronics employees have recently risen from 83 to 87. As for clients who work at SK Hynix, their scores are expected to climb from around 80 to 83—showing just how highly favored the company has become."

t: Intel turns to next-generation ASML tool to help make its laptop chips

The industry has debated at what point it makes economic sense to begin deploying the ⁠High NA tools, which likely will be needed by chipmakers in the future as they continue to shrink the atomic-sized features that make up chips.

t: Asian chip stocks slide as China competition fears rattle AI trade
desc: STORY::: Why are Asian chip stocks tumbling amid new competition from China?:: July 28, 2026/Singapore:: Gregor Stuart Hunter/Market Correspondent"So the market has a new chip champion this week and it's CXMT, which raised $8.6 billion in a listing in Shanghai on Monday and then promptly rallied almost 500%, vaulting it into the ranks of some of the biggest companies on earth. It's now the biggest listed company in mainland China. It's bigger than MasterCard, it's bigger than Intel.""So why are Asian chip stocks tumbling amid this new competition from China? It really boils down to the arrival of this new entrant in the market that, first of all, has just raised a load of capital to expand, and second of all if you're an investor and you like the chip theme, you probably own a lot of Asian chip makers to begin with. So if you want to buy CXMT's shares, you're gonna have to make room for something in the portfolio, which probably means dumping Samsung or SK Hynix or TSMC or another name like that. And that's ultimately why the market seems to be having such trouble digesting this new arrival.""But for now, they'll have to wait as it's listed in Shanghai, that means most global investors won't have immediate access to the stock.":: How does Apple's lobbying fit into this?"So Apple has been asking the Trump administration reportedly for a bit of leeway in terms of what memory it can use in its products. Remember that Apple recently had to hike prices across a range of its devices, principally because the cost of memory is getting so high because it's also competing with the AI industry for memory chips. On the other hand, a US company like Micron is quite keen to keep Chinese memory out of US supply chains, so is putting equal amounts of pressure in the opposite direction. The Trump administration is caught in the middle.":: Is the AI-driven semiconductor rally sustainable?"A lot of investors have been worried about a question that essentially boils down to how much debt is being racked up by the tech sector to fund its build out of AI tools. And more importantly, how is that gonna be paid back?""We'll get some indication from the big tech companies this week as to how that expansion is going. We've got earnings coming up from Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, and Apple, as well as some of TSMC suppliers. And they should give us an indication of how much capital expenditure they expect. How much more money, in short, are they gonna keep putting into AI throughout the next few years?"

t: Wall Street Sold Off Intel After Its Earnings. But the Company Is Setting Up a Monster 2027.
desc: In this segment of the AI Investor Podcast from 24/7 Wall St., co-hosts Eric Bleeker and Austin Smith work through Intel's quarter and the whipsaw price action around it. Bleeker opens with the trading pattern as a microcosm of the month: Intel rose 10% after hours on the report, then fell roughly 30% over the following days, leaving it down 34% on the month at the end of last week. Yet, zoomed out, the stock is up 134% year to date and still more than double its post-February level, while most momentum names have given back their post-February gains entirely. He reads that as evidence Intel remains a structural winner. Bleeker credits two calls made earlier. The first was the rise of CPUs, which he says is playing out more forcefully than expected, with Intel's CPU prices up 48%. The second, and the one that matters more long term, is the foundry business. Intel guided 14A to volume production in 2028, which Bleeker takes as on track. Wall Street's disappointment centered on Intel declining to name customers, but Bleeker argues that silence is rational: a company shifting volume away from Taiwan Semiconductor has no interest in publicizing it and risking its existing allocation. What Intel needs, he notes, is wafer customers rather than packaging work, and he sees potential majors like Google drifting toward it. Smith agrees the non-disclosure is sensible and adds that these are not phantom customers. He points to reporting on xAI and the widely covered Apple arrangement as reasonably well established, meaning Intel gains little by confirming them publicly.

t: Meta’s Muse Is BLOWING Minds…. But At What Cost?

Unlike previous consumer AI models that struggled with resource limits, Muse delivers secure, sandboxed personal environments with dedicated virtual machines and private browsers to keep your data completely locked down. With active users skyrocketing at a historic pace and even major publications praising its seamless capabilities, consumer-agentic AI has officially arrived.
